# Lists {#sec-lists} *This chapter is about lists and dictionaries that are Python values that can contain other Python values. Lists and dictionaries let you build relationships between values, which is what data structures represent.* ## Lists For many kinds of data, the order of things is important. Just like the order of characters is important for the meaning of the text in a string, we sometimes want to specify the order of other things because the relative order of items in the list has some meaning. It could be a grocery list where you have listed the things to buy in the order you get to them in the supermarket. This is where Python lists are helpful. When you print a list, it nicely shows all the values it contains. ::: {#cell-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} grocery_list = ["salad", "canned beans", "milk", 'beer', 'candy'] print(grocery_list) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['salad', 'canned beans', 'milk', 'beer', 'candy'] ``` ::: ::: Unlike strings that can only store the order of characters, lists can contain *any* kind of values, and you can mix different types of values in any way you like. Here is a list that contains an integer, a boolean, a string, and a list: ::: {#cell-3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} mixed_list = [42, True, 'programming', [1, 2, 3] ] ``` ::: By now, you have probably guessed you will make a list with two square brackets. Between them, you can put values with commas in between. A list is a *container* of other values, and the value of the list itself does not depend on the values it contains. This makes sense. Otherwise, an empty list would not have a value: ::: {#cell-5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_list = [] ``` ::: You can add single values to the end of a list using the `append` method of lists. Try it out: ::: {#cell-7 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} desserts = [] print(desserts) desserts.append('Crepe suzette') print(desserts) desserts.append('Tiramisu') print(desserts) desserts.append('Creme brulee') print(desserts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [] ['Crepe suzette'] ['Crepe suzette', 'Tiramisu'] ['Crepe suzette', 'Tiramisu', 'Creme brulee'] ``` ::: ::: If you have a list you want to add to the end of another list, you use the `extend` method: ::: {#cell-9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} cheeses = ['Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] desserts.extend(cheeses) print(desserts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['Crepe suzette', 'Tiramisu', 'Creme brulee', 'Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] ``` ::: ::: Notice how `append` and `extend` *modifies* the existing list instead of producing a new list with the added element. #### Exercise Do you think this will work? ::: {#cell-11 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} cheeses = ['Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] print(cheeses) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] ``` ::: ::: Surprised? Code inside parentheses, brackets, and braces can span several lines, sometimes making your code easier to read. #### Exercise You use the' in' operator to test if a value is in a list. Try this: ::: {#cell-13 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('Tiramisu' in desserts) print('Meatloaf' in desserts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True False ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise You can concatenate two lists to produce a new joined list. Make sure you figure out how this works before you try it. Then, experiment with changing the lists. Can you concatenate two empty lists? ::: {#cell-15 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} some_list = [1, 2, 3] another_list = [7, 8, 9] merged_list = some_list + another_list print(merged_list) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9] ``` ::: ::: This is yet another example of how the functionality of Python objects lets them "know" how to behave under different circumstances, such as when adding two objects (see @sec-add_method). #### Exercise What do you think is printed here? Make sure you figure out how you think this works before you try it out. What does the `append` method return? ::: {#cell-17 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_list = [] x = my_list.append(7) print(x) print(my_list) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None [7] ``` ::: ::: ## Indexing and slicing lists Now you know how to make lists, but to work with the values in lists, you must also know how to access the individual values a list contains. Fortunately, indexing lists work just like indexing strings: Each value in a list is identified by an *index* exactly like each character in a string: ::: {#cell-19 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} numbers = [7, 4, 6, 2, 8, 1] print("first value is", numbers[0]) print("second value is", numbers[1]) print("third value is", numbers[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` first value is 7 second value is 4 third value is 6 ``` ::: ::: Notice that the function `len` can also compute the length of a list. So you also get the last value in a list like this: ::: {#cell-21 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} numbers = [7, 4, 6, 2, 8, 1] last_index = len(numbers)-1 print("Last element is", numbers[last_index]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Last element is 1 ``` ::: ::: If you want a sub-list of values from a list (we also call that a *slice*), you specify a start index and an end index separated by a colon, just like with strings: ::: {#cell-23 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(numbers[1:4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [4, 6, 2] ``` ::: ::: When you run that, you can see that `numbers[1:4]` is substituted for `[4, 6, 2]`, so the slicing operation produces a new list of the specified values. #### Exercise What do these two expressions reduce to? ::: {#cell-25 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17][2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` 13 ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise What is printed here? Do all the substitution and reduction steps and compare them to the exercise above. ::: {#cell-27 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] print(l[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 13 ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise What is printed here? Do all the substitution and reduction steps — and do them twice. Next week, you will be happy you did. ::: {#cell-29 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} numbers = [1,2,3] i = 0 print(number[i]) i = 1 print(number[i]) i = 2 print(number[i]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Make up your mind and try out the code below: ::: {#cell-31 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] l[4] = "Donald" print(l) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [11, 12, 13, 14, 'Donald', 16, 17] ``` ::: ::: Were you surprised by what happened? Compare to @sec-immutable_strings. Lists are not immutable like strings, and you can replace values by assigning a new value to an index in the list. #### Exercise With your knowledge of slicing, what do you think is printed below: ::: {#cell-33 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] print(l[:3]) print(l[3:]) print(l[:]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [11, 12, 13] [14, 15, 16, 17] [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise What do you think happens when you specify an index that does not correspond to a value in the list: ::: {#cell-35 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] print(l[7]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
IndexError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[18], line 2
      1 l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]
----> 2 print(l[7])

IndexError: list index out of range
``` ::: ::: ::: Read and understand the error message. Does it ring a bell? #### Exercise Do you also get an error when you specify a slice where the end is too high? Try it out: ::: {#cell-37 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] print(l[4:99]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [15, 16, 17] ``` ::: ::: I guess that is also worth remembering. #### Exercise Which value in a list named `l` does this expression reduce to? ::: {#cell-39 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} l[len(l)-1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` 17 ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise If you do not like Emmentaler, you can delete it. What does the `del` keyword do? ::: {#cell-41 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} cheeses = ['Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] print(cheeses) del cheeses[1] print(cheeses) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['Gorgonzola', 'Emmentaler', 'Camembert'] ['Gorgonzola', 'Camembert'] ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Because intervals are "ends exclusive," we can compute the length of a slice as `end - start`: ::: {#cell-43 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [7, 4, 6, 2, 8, 1] start = 1 end = 4 print("{} has length {}".format(l[start:end], end-start)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [4, 6, 2] has length 3 ``` ::: ::: Consider what this code would look like if ends were included in intervals. #### Exercise Another advantage of "ends exclusive" intervals is that you only need one index to split a list in two: ::: {#cell-45 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] i = 3 beginning = numbers[:i] end = numbers[i:] print(beginning + end) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] ``` ::: ::: If ends were included in intervals, this would be more complex. #### Exercise Do *all* the substitution and reduction steps in your head (or on paper) before you write any of the following code. Think carefully and decide what you think will be printed below. Remember that the *value* of a list is a container that holds other *values* in it. Then, write the code and see if you are right. If you were not, figure out what led you to the wrong conclusion. ::: {#cell-47 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = 'A' y = 'B' z = 'C' lst = [x, y, z] print(lst) x = 'Preben' print(lst) # what is printed here? lst[0] = 'Mogens' print(lst) # what is printed here? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C'] ['A', 'B', 'C'] ['Mogens', 'B', 'C'] ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Do you remember this trick from string slicing? ::: {#cell-49 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} l = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] print(l[::-1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise You can produce a list by splitting a long string into smaller parts. Think: "*Hey string, split yourself on this smaller string*". Try these variations to figure out how it works. ::: {#cell-51 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} "Homo sapiens neanderthalensis".split(" ") "Homo sapiens neanderthalensis".split('en') 'ATGCTCGTAACGACACTGCACTACTACAATAG'.split('') "1, 2, 3, 5, 3, 2, 5, 3".split(', ') "1,2,3,5,3,2,5,3".split(',') 'ATGCTCGTAACGACACTGCACTACTACAATAG'.split() "Homo sapiens neanderthalensis".split() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: Notice that the method has a default behavior when no argument is passed to it. #### Exercise You can produce a string by joining the elements of a list (if all the elements are strings, of course). Think: "*Hey string, put yourself between all the strings in this list*". ::: {#cell-53 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} "-".join(['Homo', 'sapiens', 'neanderthalensis']) "...".join(['Homo', 'sapiens', 'neanderthalensis']) "".join(['A', 'T', 'G']) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` 'ATG' ``` ::: ::: Notice how you can join something on an empty string. This is a very useful technique to turn a list of characters into a string. ## General exercises What does this expression reduce to? `'aaaaa'`, `'BaBaBa'`, or `'Banan'`. Make up your mind, and then run the expression to check. ::: {#cell-55 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} 'a'.join('Banana'.split('a')[:3] * 4)[-5:] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` 'Banan' ``` ::: :::
